name: Zipf's Law
statement: A word's frequency is inversely proportional to its rank: the second-commonest word appears about half as often as the first.
meaning: Rank all the words in a large text by how often they occur, and the frequencies fall off in a strikingly regular way — the 2nd-ranked word about half as often as the 1st, the 3rd about a third as often, and so on. A handful of words dominate usage; a vast number are individually rare.
mechanism: The relationship is a discrete power law, the close cousin of the Pareto distribution: on a log–log plot of frequency against rank the points fall roughly on a straight line of slope −1. In the million-word Brown Corpus, 'the' accounts for about 7% of all words and 'of' for about 3.5% — a near-textbook 1/rank curve. Why it arises is debated: candidates include Zipf's own 'principle of least effort', preferential-attachment growth, and the possibility that it is largely a statistical artefact.

examples.text: In English corpora, a few function words ('the', 'of', 'and') make up a large share of all tokens while most words appear rarely — the pattern Zipf first measured, and the one that still holds across languages.

The rank–size rule: a country's cities tend to have populations inversely proportional to their rank, so the third-largest city is roughly a third the size of the largest. Felix Auerbach noticed this for cities as early as 1913.
The upper tails of firm sizes and website traffic approximate the same 1/rank curve — a few giants, a long tail of small players — one of many domains where a Zipf-like distribution turns up.

variants.name: The Zipf–Mandelbrot law
variants.text: A generalisation, frequency ∝ 1/(rank + b)^a, that fits real corpora better — especially at the very top ranks, where pure Zipf tends to miss.

variants.name: The principle of least effort
variants.text: Zipf's proposed cause: speakers and hearers each minimise their effort, and the compromise between them produces the skewed frequency curve.

variants.name: A member of the power-law family
variants.text: Zipf's law is the rank–frequency face of the same skew captured by the Pareto principle and, in a different guise, by Benford's law.

whyItMatters: It is one of the most robust empirical regularities in the study of language and, more broadly, of ranked data — turning up in words, cities, firms, and web traffic alike. It tells you to expect a short, dominant head and a very long tail, and it anchors work from information retrieval to natural-language processing.

working.lead: Expect a short head and a long tail
working.text: in ranked data — words, products, users — a few items dominate and a great many are individually rare; plan for both, not for a uniform middle.
the 1/rank line is approximate and bends at the extremes; use it as a shape, not a precise formula.
a Zipf-like curve alone does not prove deep structure, since even random text can produce one — see it as a pattern to explain, not an explanation.

limits: Zipf's law is only approximate and deviates at both extremes — the very top ranks (the 'King effect', where the largest item sits off the line) and the rare-item tail, which often turns log-normal. For city sizes one study rejected it in 53 of 73 countries. Most tellingly, Wentian Li showed in 1992 that text generated by typing characters at random already produces a Zipf-like rank–frequency curve — which suggests the law may be substantially an artefact of rank–frequency plotting rather than evidence of deep linguistic structure. The regularity is robust; its cause is genuinely contested.
misreadings: It is not an exact formula, and a Zipf-like distribution does not by itself reveal anything profound about language — random text yields one too. It is a strong descriptive regularity whose underlying cause remains unsettled.
origin: Named for the linguist George Kingsley Zipf, who documented it in The Psycho-Biology of Language (1935) and developed it in Human Behavior and the Principle of Least Effort (1949). The pattern had antecedents — Jean-Baptiste Estoup (1916) and Edward Condon (1928) for words, Felix Auerbach (1913) for city sizes — which Zipf acknowledged.
